newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Thames Water focus is on strategy.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Thames Water focus is on strategy.

text.p: Thames Water, supplier of water and sewerage systems to Britain's capital, is expected to show it is focusing on shareholder value through dividend and strategy when it reports half year results on October 29.
"It should refocus on the core business. The non-core has been profoundly disappointing," said one sector analyst who asked not to be named.
Thames is forecast to turn in pretax profits of 177 to 188 million stg for the half year, up from 165 million stg previously.

Dividend payouts, which represents around a third of the total year dividend, could be generous if they take account of a 10 percent share buyback made over the summer, with analysts looking for 10.3-11.5 pence per share, up from 9.2 pence.
A change of management at the company in March, when Bill Alexander moved from head of the core business to group managing director, signalled the end of a drought for shareholders.
In June, the full year dividend was hiked 12 percent and Alexander promised to maintain those growth levels as well as putting the buyback in place.
"The key (at interims) will be the buyback as there are now fewer shares in issue," said one analyst.

A recent change to legislation removing tax breaks on buybacks and some special dividends could also prompt Thames to aim for a high increase in the ordinary payout, analysts said. But they added that the dividend rise could be more cautious if Thames, supplier to Britain's capital London, decides it wants to stay out of political fire over fat payouts in the run-up to a general election, which must be held by May 1997.
There is some pressure on the company to follow in the steps of its colleagues North West Water and Welsh Water by merging with its local electricity firm London Electricity.
Thames and London have said in the past they were working together but Alexander has ruled out a merger as not right for shareholders.
"The London Electricity questions are bound to surface again, after mergers which have produced cost savings," the sector analyst said.

The opposition Labour party, ahead of the ruling Conservatives in the polls, have already vowed to impose a one-off "windfall" tax on profits of utilities, which have been slammed for hefty dividends and bulging directors' pay packets.

At the same time, analysts hope Thames will show it is now focusing on its core business of water and sewerage after selling its design and construction ventures UTAG in Germany and PWT in the UK in October after a strategic review.
"Perhaps we will see the emergence of a new Thames Water," the analyst said.
United Utilities, formed when North West Water merged with regional electricity company Norweb earlier this year, expects to make annual cost savings of 140 million stg by the turn of the century.

Bid speculation fired utilities stocks on Friday on rumours of possible U.S. buyers for electricity firms and was fuelled further when the UK frustrated plans by Severn Trent and Wessex Water to bid for South West Water.
